ExtractionPrompt:
Perform named entity and referential mention recognition over the complete user directive. The purpose is to identify every span whose meaning must be resolved so a downstream agent can understand the directive without ambiguity. Include meaningful named or referential objects, systems, products, applications, repositories, files, directories, projects, solutions, websites, pages, UI regions, controls, documents, records, databases, organizations, people, places, sessions, tools, actions, and other domain entities. Include meaningful claims or relational phrases only when they must remain annotated for the directive to make sense; do not annotate incidental grammar, generic filler, or whole sentences when a focused exact span is sufficient.

Return only the complete source text annotated with the established ontology grammar. Preserve every source character exactly and in order, including apostrophes, quotation marks, dashes, whitespace, capitalization, and spelling. Mark each unresolved exact source span as [verbatim source span]{unresolved; grounding=needed}. Prefer precise, non-overlapping spans; include repeated mentions when they independently refer. Do not search the ontology, choose prototypes, accept identity, organize a hierarchy, or perform physical grounding. Do not return JSON, prose, headings, code fences, IDs, offsets, or an explanation.
BindingPrompt:
Evaluate all unresolved spans and all supplied candidates together against the meaning of the complete user directive. Build the most coherent interpretation of the whole message rather than selecting each span independently. Candidate similarity and returned order are retrieval evidence, not identity confidence. Context, entity type, ownership, containment, co-reference, the user's requested action, and compatibility among selected entities must all support a binding. Natural-language determiners, capitalization, and phrasing need not exactly match a prototype name.

For each unresolved span, choose at most one exact supplied prototype. Replace it with [[protoscript:<exact supplied prototype>|<exact source span>]] when the directive provides enough contextual evidence to identify the intended ontology object or system family and the candidate's type fits the role of the mention. Prefer the candidate that represents the object actually being discussed (for example, the relevant user-facing system surface rather than an incidental implementation component). Do not require absolute certainty when one candidate is materially better supported by the complete frame. Leave the existing unresolved grammar unchanged when candidates remain genuinely ambiguous or none is good. Never invent a prototype, select a candidate merely because it is first or has the highest score, or silently force every span to bind. Preserve any binding already present in the grammar as authoritative, including user-selected bindings. Do not perform physical-object grounding, ontology writes, or hierarchy organization.

Return only the complete grammar from the <grammar> block. Preserve every source character, span boundary, and existing annotation exactly unless replacing an unresolved annotation with a supported binding. Do not return JSON, prose, headings, wrapper tags, code fences, IDs, offsets, relationships, claims, or an explanation.
GroundingPrompt:
Ground the complete directive into the narrowest stable physical or semantic objects supported by exhaustive tool-assisted research. Preserve the complete grammar and existing authoritative bindings. Return grammar only.

You must inspect every annotated item in the grammar, including:
- each unresolved annotation with `grounding=needed`, whether or not it has lookup candidates;
- each existing `[[protoscript:...]]` binding, because a semantic binding can still need a physical/file/DOM/line grounding;
- each related span that depends on another span for context, such as sections, cards, attachments, document-signing areas, and lead/page records.

For each annotated item, either replace/add the annotation with the best defensible grounded reference or leave the item exactly as-is when research cannot prove a target. Do not silently skip an item. Do not treat existing protoscript bindings as already physically grounded. Use available tools to inspect candidate resources, source files, rendered page structure, DOM/text/line evidence, logs, or other direct evidence before grounding. Exhaust the plausible concrete targets before leaving an item unresolved.

A grounded reference has a resource and may have typed locators inside that resource:
[[file:<path>|<label>]]
[[file:<path>::dom-id=<id>|<label>]]
[[file:<path>::selector=<url-encoded-selector>|<label>]]
[[file:<path>::heading=<url-encoded-heading>|<label>]]
[[file:<path>::lines=<start>-<end>|<label>]]
[[file:<path>::text=<url-encoded-text-quote>|<label>]]
[[file:<path-to-csharp>::class=<url-encoded-class-name>|<label>]]
[[file:<path-to-csharp>::method=<url-encoded-method-name>|<label>]]
[[file:<path-to-csharp>::class=<url-encoded-class-name>&method=<url-encoded-method-name>|<label>]]

The text after | is only a display label; it does not identify an object inside the resource. If research identifies a DOM element, section, collection, heading, class, method, symbol, line range, quotation, attachment, or other internal object, encode that identity with typed locators. Use multiple locators when they jointly identify the object. URL-encode locator values containing spaces or reserved characters. Prefer provider-native IDs, code symbols, DOM IDs, bookmarks, and explicit stable grounding IDs over selectors, headings, text quotes, and line ranges. Use a bare resource only when the mention denotes the complete resource or no narrower locator can be verified. Do not ground a runtime record to source code merely because the code renders it. Leave a mention unresolved when no defensible target exists. Do not invent resources or locators.
